It's a worn-down suffix, *-old* from something murkier, possibly *-hold* or a lost word entirely. Etymologists actually shrug at the second half. That's the part I like. A word everyone uses, every day, to mean the strip of wood or stone you cross to enter a room—and half of it is a question mark. We stand on it confidently without knowing what we're standing on.

*Thresh*, though, that part is solid. To thresh is to beat grain, to separate the wheat from the chaff by trampling or flailing. So the threshold might once have been the place where threshing happened, or the board that held the threshed grain in while you swept—a little lip at the bottom of the door. The crossing-place was originally a *containing* place. A barrier disguised as a passage, or the reverse.

And the sound of it. *Threh-* starts soft and breathy, that *th* that English speakers don't even notice is hard to make—tongue against teeth, air pushed through—and then it collapses into *-shold*, which lands heavier, more closed. The word itself moves from open to shut. From breath to stone. You exhale the first syllable and then the door closes on the second.

There's a directionality baked into *thr-*, a passing-through that's never quite frictionless.

Which loops me back, accidentally, to the threshold being a place of passage. Did the sound do that? Did the *thr-* recruit *threshold* into the family of forward-motion words even though its meaning came from grain-beating? You're either in or out, arrived or departed; the language gives you the line but not the lingering on it. *Liminal* is the closest, but it's borrowed, academic, came late and from anthropology.
